newsitem.title: KENYA: Sudanese rebels deny Khartoum opened Uganda front.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese rebels deny Khartoum opened Uganda front.

text.p: Sudanese rebels denied on Wednesday the government army had opened a new front near Sudan's border with Uganda and said rebel forces were advancing on a strategic dam.

The Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) said Khartoum was "peddling lies" by saying on Sunday that its troops attacked a rebel base near the border with Uganda following clashes in eastern Sudan near the borders with Ethiopia and Eritrea.
"No fighting has taken place in that area since successful SPLA operations...last year," said a SPLA statement, adding the site of the attack as reported by Khartoum did not even exist.
State television quoted Sudan's information minister on Sunday as saying the army killed rebels at Lokia, nar the southern town of Torit 75 km (47 miles) from the Uganda border.
"Such a place (Lokia) does not exist in the Sudan. This is therefore another attempt to bolster the image and morale of the NIF (National Islamic Front) mujahideen (holy warriors)," the SPLA said.
"The claim by the NIF regime there was fighting on Sunday January 26, 1997, in the Blue Nile area where they allegedly killed 300 Ethiopian troops is equally untrue," it added.
Sudanese state television said on Tuesday the army killed 24 rebels and destroyed bases in weekend fighting in Western Equatoria, which is almost entirely controlled by rebel forces.
The SPLA on Wednesday accused government forces and allied militiamen of attacking Lohila village just south of Torit on January 24 and killing seven civilians and wounding many more.
"Our forces are in high morale and are steadily advancing towards Damazin and Roseires so as to achieve the goal to overthrow the NIF regime and institute a democratic system," it added.
The rebels say their aim is to take the southeastern town of Damazin near the strategic Roseires Dam and hydroelectric plant, which provides Khartoum with 80 percent of its electricity.

There have been no independent accounts of the fighting since the National Democratic Alliance including the SPLA launched an offensive in eastern Sudan on January 12. It is difficult to assess the veracity of reports by the two sides.
Khartoum says Eritrean and Ethiopian troops are fighting alongside the rebels but both countries have denied involvement.
SPLA leader John Garang says the opposition alliance's strategy is to overthrow the government through war in the east and south of Sudan and a popular mass uprising in Khartoum.

But a Western diplomat in Nairobi said he doubted the rebels could seize Damazin and Roseires because they were too important to the government and there was no apparent chance the rebel offensive would unleash an uprising in the capital.
"The goal of this current offensive is clearly political pressure to get Khartoum either to collapse or at least to push it into some serious negotiations," the diplomat told Reuters.
"They want something this year...but Khartoum will try and buy time," he added. "The major obstacle for the rebels however is the presence of a recalcitrant or worse Hassan al-Turabi."
Turabi is Sudan's speaker of parliament and the Islamist idealogue behind the military-dominated government in Khartoum.

"At this point it looks like Turabi will tough it out...he genuinely believes he can ride this bucking bronco to a standstill but his losing his cool recently indicates he views it seriously," said the diplomat, who declined to be identified.
